doc.title: Billy Bauer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: Teaching guitar: finger patterns versus knowing the notes
summary: Bauer describes his small school, urging students to sing the lines of players like Lester Young and to learn where notes are on the fingerboard; about eighteen students and a weakened voice from singing with them.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well it isn’t a big school, but what I do, I mean if I had to earn a living I couldn’t do it. But being the way I am, like at this part of my life, I like to see people and how they want to do things, these fellas take — some of them throw away everything. They think they’re going to be big stars or something. And they make their own record dates and they put everything they’ve got into this. So I try to tell them, you know, go ahead. It’s your turn to roll the dice. And then they say how did you — I says don’t do what I did. You know you’ve got your own life and I generally, when they get doing it they want to copy, and I try to tell them listen to other people that came before, like Lester Young or somebody like that, and sing their part. Don’t play it. Because on guitar, I don’t know if you’re familiar with guitar, but guitar, you get set fingerings and you’re really not improvising, you’re playing the same fingers. You know like for instance I say do you know all your scales? This is the first time they come. Either they say no or yes. But if they say yes, I say well all right, play it. So they play it. I say play it in the fifth position. They play in the fifth position but they just move up, instead of playing G they’re up like the B flat key but it’s the same fingering. So I try to explain to them that they’re playing their finger patterns — not that you can get away, guitar is a very, the fingerboard is odd. Like to read.
So when you said that they’re just moving their fingers up a few positions and then playing that they don’t know the notes that they’re playing? Is that what you’re saying?

That’s right. They’ve got a finger pattern. Oh I know it’s a third — they can hear it — but they don’t know. So I say now if you’re going to come to me, do you want to learn how to read? And when they say yes, then I say well then you have to know where everything is. And some of them are piano players and saxophone, violin, they can read music. But they can’t find it on the guitar. See so that’s my little project, is to shows them different ways of learning the guitar, doing it in the head, that they can sing in their head. Anyway, what was that question?
We’re talking about — how many students does your business have right now?

Oh it does vary, about I guess most of the time it’s around eighteen, something like that. If I teach three hours or four hours a day, you see, I’m losing my voice now. I had to go the doctor last year because I used to lose my voice so much I couldn’t talk because I sing with them. [scats] All that kind of singing. See so I’m doing that all day and he says there’s nothing wrong, like you’ve not got anything wrong like cancer of the throat, but you’ve got weak whatever this is called, throat muscles.

Yeah. Like they’re weak. So that’s why everybody recommends — I say hello, they say oh Billy. And I don’t know them that well. See so I’ve got a very distinct sound, not that it’s good but it’s different. Well anyway.
